history.q: In which year did Parisians storm the Bastille?
history.fact: The Bastille held only seven prisoners when it was stormed. The date, 14 July, is now France's national holiday.

history.q: Which military leader crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804?
history.fact: Napoleon was born in Ajaccio, Corsica, in 1769, just a year after Genoa handed the island over to France.

history.q: Which young peasant woman helped lift the English siege of Orléans in 1429?
history.fact: Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in Rouen in 1431, aged about 19. She was made a saint in 1920 and is a patron saint of France.

history.q: Which French king was known as the "Sun King"?
history.fact: Louis XIV reigned for 72 years (1643-1715), one of the longest reigns in European history. He moved the royal court to Versailles in 1682.

history.q: Which queen, the wife of Louis XVI, was guillotined in 1793?
history.fact: Marie Antoinette was born an Archduchess of Austria. There is no evidence that she ever said "Let them eat cake".

history.q: On which French coast did Allied forces land on D-Day, 6 June 1944?
history.fact: The five landing beaches were code-named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword. It is still the largest seaborne invasion in history.

history.q: Which Frankish king was crowned Emperor by the Pope in Rome on Christmas Day in the year 800?
history.fact: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne in St Peter's Basilica. His empire covered much of western Europe, and he is sometimes called the "Father of Europe".

history.q: At which battle in 1815 was Napoleon finally defeated?
history.fact: Waterloo is in present-day Belgium. Napoleon was then exiled to Saint Helena, a remote island in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.

history.q: Which 1598 decree by Henry IV granted rights and religious tolerance to French Protestants?
history.fact: Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685 with the Edict of Fontainebleau, and hundreds of thousands of Huguenots fled abroad.

history.q: Who was crowned King of the Franks in 987, founding the Capetian dynasty?
history.fact: Capetian kings and their branches, the Valois and the Bourbons, ruled France for most of the next 800 years.

history.q: What name is given to the period of the French Revolution, in 1793-94, when thousands were executed by guillotine?
history.fact: Maximilien Robespierre, one of the Terror's leading figures, was himself guillotined in July 1794.

history.q: Which French king was guillotined in January 1793?
history.fact: Louis XVI was executed on the Place de la Révolution in Paris, the square now known as the Place de la Concorde.

history.q: In which year was Paris liberated from German occupation in the Second World War?
history.fact: Paris was liberated on 25 August 1944. General Leclerc's Free French 2nd Armoured Division was among the first troops to enter the city.

history.q: Which Scandinavian raiders settled in northern France and gave Normandy its name?
history.fact: In 911 the Viking leader Rollo was granted land around Rouen by King Charles the Simple. His descendants included William the Conqueror.

history.q: Which long conflict between England and France lasted, on and off, from 1337 to 1453?
history.fact: Despite its name, the Hundred Years' War actually lasted 116 years, with long truces between the bouts of fighting.

history.q: To which Mediterranean island was Napoleon first exiled in 1814?
history.fact: Napoleon escaped from Elba in February 1815 and returned to power in Paris, beginning the period known as the Hundred Days.

history.q: Which marshal headed the collaborationist Vichy regime from 1940 to 1944?
history.fact: Pétain was sentenced to death after the war, but de Gaulle commuted the sentence to life imprisonment. He died on the Île d'Yeu in 1951.

history.q: Which 1916 First World War battle in north-eastern France became a lasting symbol of French resistance?
history.fact: The Battle of Verdun lasted about ten months, from February to December 1916, making it one of the longest battles in history.

history.q: Which French explorer founded Quebec City in 1608?
history.fact: Champlain is often called the "Father of New France". He crossed the Atlantic more than 20 times during his career.

history.q: Which vast North American territory did Napoleon sell to the United States in 1803?
history.fact: The Louisiana Purchase cost about $15 million and roughly doubled the size of the young United States.

history.q: What name is given to the 1572 massacre of Protestants that began in Paris?
history.fact: The killings began on 24 August 1572, only days after the wedding of the Protestant Henry of Navarre to the Catholic Margaret of Valois.

history.q: Which revolutionary government briefly ruled Paris in the spring of 1871?
history.fact: The Commune lasted about two months before government troops crushed it during "la Semaine sanglante" (Bloody Week) in May 1871.

history.q: Which army officer was wrongly convicted of treason in 1894, sparking a scandal that divided France?
history.fact: In 1898 the novelist Émile Zola defended Dreyfus in a famous open letter headlined "J'accuse...!". Dreyfus was fully cleared in 1906.

history.q: At which 1415 battle did Henry V's English army defeat a much larger French force?
history.fact: The battle was fought on St Crispin's Day, 25 October, and English longbowmen played a decisive part in the victory.

history.q: Who reigned from 1830 to 1848 as the last king to rule France?
history.fact: Louis-Philippe was styled "King of the French". Overthrown in 1848, he fled to England under the name "Mr Smith".

technology.q: Which French scientist gave his name to pasteurisation, a way of using heat to kill microbes in food?
technology.fact: Pasteur also developed a rabies vaccine. In 1885 it was first given to Joseph Meister, a nine-year-old boy who had been bitten by a rabid dog, and he survived.

technology.q: Which scientist, working in Paris, became the first person to win two Nobel Prizes?
technology.fact: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911. She is still the only person to win in two different sciences.

technology.q: Who invented a raised-dot reading and writing system for blind people?
technology.fact: Louis Braille lost his sight after an accident in his father's workshop at the age of three. He created his system as a teenager.

technology.q: Which brothers held one of the first public screenings of projected films, in Paris in 1895?
technology.fact: The screening was held at the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines on 28 December 1895, using their Cinématographe.

technology.q: Which French brothers pioneered the hot-air balloon, leading to the first crewed free flight in 1783?
technology.fact: Before any people flew, a test flight at Versailles in September 1783 carried a sheep, a duck and a rooster.

technology.q: Which supersonic airliner did France and Britain develop together?
technology.fact: Concorde first flew from Toulouse in 1969. It cruised at about twice the speed of sound and could cross the Atlantic in about three and a half hours.

technology.q: Which French chemist, often called the "father of modern chemistry", named oxygen and hydrogen?
technology.fact: Lavoisier also worked as a royal tax collector, and for that he was guillotined in 1794 during the Reign of Terror.

technology.q: Which unit of electric current is named after a French physicist?
technology.fact: André-Marie Ampère was largely self-taught. His name is one of 72 scientists' and engineers' names engraved around the Eiffel Tower.

technology.q: Which French physicist discovered radioactivity in 1896 while experimenting with uranium salts?
technology.fact: Becquerel shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie and Pierre Curie. The SI unit of radioactivity, the becquerel, is named after him.

technology.q: Which French high-speed train set the world speed record for a conventional train, 574.8 km/h, in 2007?
technology.fact: TGV stands for Train à Grande Vitesse ("high-speed train"). Its first passenger service began in 1981, between Paris and Lyon.

technology.q: Which French ocean explorer co-invented the Aqua-Lung, an early scuba diving system, in 1943?
technology.fact: Cousteau developed the Aqua-Lung with the engineer Émile Gagnan. His documentary "The Silent World" won the top prize at Cannes in 1956.

technology.q: Whose engineering company designed and built the Eiffel Tower?
technology.fact: Gustave Eiffel's company also designed the iron framework hidden inside the Statue of Liberty in New York.

technology.q: Which European aircraft manufacturer has its main base in Toulouse?
technology.fact: The Airbus A380, the world's largest passenger airliner, made its first flight from Toulouse in April 2005.

technology.q: Which system of measurement, based on the metre and the kilogram, was developed in Revolutionary France?
technology.fact: The metre was first defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator, measured along the meridian through Paris.

technology.q: Which French thinker, famous for "I think, therefore I am", gave his name to Cartesian coordinates?
technology.fact: Descartes died in Stockholm in 1650, during a cold winter spent tutoring Queen Christina of Sweden.

technology.q: Which French artist and inventor announced the daguerreotype photographic process in 1839?
technology.fact: Daguerre's late partner Nicéphore Niépce made the oldest surviving camera photograph, a view from a window, in about 1826-27.

technology.q: Which French mathematician built an early mechanical calculator, the Pascaline, in the 1640s?
technology.fact: Pascal built his calculator as a teenager to help his father, a tax official. The SI unit of pressure, the pascal, is named after him.

technology.q: Which energy source produces most of France's electricity?
technology.fact: France has more than 50 nuclear reactors, which usually supply around two-thirds of its electricity.

technology.q: Which French mathematician's "Last Theorem" remained unproven for more than 350 years?
technology.fact: Fermat wrote in a book margin that he had a proof too large to fit there. Andrew Wiles finally proved the theorem in 1994.

technology.q: Which French carmaker launched the 2CV in 1948?
technology.fact: The 2CV was designed for farmers. The brief reportedly asked for a car that could cross a ploughed field carrying a basket of eggs without breaking them.

technology.q: Which French physician invented the stethoscope in 1816?
technology.fact: Laennec's first stethoscope was a rolled-up tube of paper, which he used so he would not have to press his ear to a young patient's chest.

technology.q: Which French physicist laid the foundations of thermodynamics in his 1824 work on the motive power of heat?
technology.fact: Sadi Carnot published only one book in his lifetime. He died of cholera in 1832 at the age of 36.

technology.q: Which physicist demonstrated the rotation of the Earth with a giant pendulum in Paris in 1851?
technology.fact: Foucault hung a 67-metre pendulum from the dome of the Panthéon. A replica still swings there today.

technology.q: Which French mathematician, known for his work on heat flow, is credited with first describing the greenhouse effect in the 1820s?
technology.fact: Fourier also served as a scientist on Napoleon's expedition to Egypt in 1798 and later became a prefect of the department of Isère.

technology.q: Which French inventor built the first self-propelled road vehicle, a steam-powered carriage, in 1769?
technology.fact: Cugnot's "fardier à vapeur" was designed to haul artillery. A version of it is preserved in the Musée des Arts et Métiers in Paris.

art.q: Which Impressionist painted the "Water Lilies" series in his garden at Giverny?
art.fact: Impressionism got its name from Monet's 1872 painting "Impression, Sunrise". A critic used the word as an insult.

art.q: Who wrote the novel "Les Misérables" (1862)?
art.fact: Hugo also wrote "Notre-Dame de Paris" (The Hunchback of Notre-Dame). Its success helped lead to the cathedral's 19th-century restoration.

art.q: Which Paris museum, once a royal palace, is home to the "Mona Lisa"?
art.fact: The Louvre's glass pyramid entrance, designed by the architect I. M. Pei, opened in 1989. Many Parisians objected to it at first.

art.q: Which French sculptor created "The Thinker"?
art.fact: "The Thinker" was first designed for Rodin's "Gates of Hell", where the figure shows the poet Dante thinking about his great poem.

art.q: Who wrote "The Three Musketeers"?
art.fact: Dumas's father, born in Saint-Domingue (now Haiti), became a general in the French Revolutionary army. He was one of the first generals of African descent.

art.q: Which singer, nicknamed "the Little Sparrow", made "La Vie en rose" famous?
art.fact: Piaf wrote the lyrics of "La Vie en rose" herself in 1945. "Piaf" is a slang word for a sparrow.

art.q: Which composer wrote the piano piece "Clair de lune"?
art.fact: "Clair de lune" is part of Debussy's "Suite bergamasque", published in 1905. It takes its title from a poem by Paul Verlaine.

art.q: Which classic French dish of beef slowly braised in red wine comes from Burgundy?
art.fact: In 2010 UNESCO added the "gastronomic meal of the French", with its courses, wine pairings and table rituals, to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

art.q: Which director's 1959 film "The 400 Blows" helped launch the French New Wave?
art.fact: Truffaut won Best Director at the 1959 Cannes Film Festival for the film, which drew on memories of his own troubled childhood.

art.q: Which poet published "Les Fleurs du mal" in 1857?
art.fact: After an obscenity trial in 1857, six of its poems were banned. The ban was not officially lifted until 1949.

art.q: Which French author and pilot wrote "The Little Prince" (1943)?
art.fact: Saint-Exupéry disappeared in July 1944 while flying a reconnaissance mission over the Mediterranean, a year after the book came out.

art.q: Which Montmartre cabaret, famous for its cancan dancers, has a red windmill on its roof?
art.fact: The Moulin Rouge opened in 1889. Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec made posters for it and painted many of its dancers.

art.q: Which French author wrote "Around the World in Eighty Days"?
art.fact: Jules Verne is one of the most translated authors in history. In the novel, Phileas Fogg wins his bet because travelling east gained him a day.

art.q: Which film festival on the French Riviera awards the Palme d'Or?
art.fact: The first Cannes Film Festival was planned for 1939 but was cancelled when war broke out. It was finally held in 1946.

art.q: Which French Impressionist is famous for his paintings and sculptures of ballet dancers?
art.fact: When Degas showed his sculpture "Little Dancer Aged Fourteen" in 1881, its real fabric tutu and real hair shocked many critics.

art.q: Which Paris opera house is the setting of Gaston Leroux's novel "The Phantom of the Opera"?
art.fact: The Palais Garnier sits above an underground water tank that inspired the Phantom's lake. Marc Chagall painted its ceiling in 1964.

art.q: Which playwright wrote the comedy "Tartuffe" (1664)?
art.fact: Molière fell ill on stage in 1673 while playing the lead in his own play "The Imaginary Invalid", and he died a few hours later.

art.q: Which French Post-Impressionist is famous for his paintings of Tahiti?
art.fact: In 1888 Gauguin lived with Vincent van Gogh in Arles. Their stormy weeks together ended with Van Gogh cutting off part of his ear.

art.q: Which composer wrote "Boléro" (1928)?
art.fact: British ice dancers Torvill and Dean skated to "Boléro" when they won Olympic gold in 1984, earning a string of perfect 6.0 scores.

art.q: Which composer wrote the opera "Carmen" (1875)?
art.fact: Bizet died at just 36, about three months after "Carmen" opened, so he never knew it would become one of the most performed operas in the world.

art.q: Who painted "Liberty Leading the People" (1830)?
art.fact: The painting celebrates the July Revolution of 1830. Its bare-breasted figure of Liberty helped shape the image of Marianne.

art.q: Who wrote the novel "Madame Bovary" (1857)?
art.fact: Flaubert was put on trial for offending public morals in 1857, the same year as Baudelaire, but unlike the poet he was acquitted.

art.q: Which author wrote the vast novel "In Search of Lost Time"?
art.fact: Its most famous scene has the narrator dip a madeleine cake in tea, and the taste brings back a flood of childhood memories.

art.q: Which painter was the leading figure of Fauvism, known for bold, unnatural colour?
art.fact: Late in life, unable to stand for long after surgery, Matisse created his famous paper cut-outs, "painting with scissors".

art.q: Which architect designed the Villa Savoye at Poissy, a landmark of modernism completed in 1931?
art.fact: Le Corbusier was born Charles-Édouard Jeanneret in Switzerland. He also designed the Unité d'Habitation housing block in Marseille.

politics.q: What is the official motto of the French Republic?
politics.fact: The wartime Vichy regime replaced the motto with "Travail, famille, patrie". "Liberté, égalité, fraternité" was restored after the Liberation.

politics.q: What is the official residence of the President of France?
politics.fact: The President lives in the Élysée Palace. The Prime Minister lives nearby at the Hôtel Matignon, and the Senate meets in the Luxembourg Palace.

politics.q: Who led the Free French during the Second World War and later founded the Fifth Republic?
politics.fact: On 18 June 1940 de Gaulle spoke on the BBC from London, calling on the French to keep fighting. That broadcast is known as the Appeal of 18 June.

politics.q: What is the name of the French national anthem?
politics.fact: Rouget de Lisle wrote it in Strasbourg in 1792. It is named after volunteers from Marseille who sang it as they marched into Paris.

politics.q: In which year was France's Fifth Republic established?
politics.fact: The 1958 constitution created a powerful presidency. Since a referendum in 1962, the President has been elected directly by the people.

politics.q: How long is the term of the French President, as it has been since 2002?
politics.fact: The President used to serve a seven-year term (the "septennat"). Voters chose a five-year term in a referendum in 2000.

politics.q: Under which President did France abolish the death penalty in 1981?
politics.fact: Justice Minister Robert Badinter championed abolition. France's last execution, by guillotine, took place in 1977.

politics.q: What is the lower house of the French Parliament called?
politics.fact: The National Assembly's 577 deputies meet in the Palais Bourbon, on the left bank of the Seine.

politics.q: In which year were French women granted the right to vote?
politics.fact: The right was granted in April 1944. French women voted for the first time a year later, in the municipal elections of April 1945.

politics.q: Which French body decides whether laws comply with the constitution?
politics.fact: Its members are nicknamed "les Sages" (the wise ones). Former Presidents of the Republic are entitled to sit on it for life.

politics.q: Who was President of France from 2012 to 2017?
politics.fact: Hollande became the first President of the Fifth Republic not to seek a second term when he decided not to run again in 2017.

politics.q: What are the three colours of the French flag?
politics.fact: The tricolour dates from the Revolution and is traditionally said to combine the blue and red of Paris with the white of the monarchy.

politics.q: What is the name of the female figure who symbolises the French Republic?
politics.fact: Busts of Marianne stand in town halls across France. Some have been modelled on famous women, including Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve.

politics.q: What is the upper house of the French Parliament called?
politics.fact: French senators are not elected directly by the public but by an electoral college made up mostly of local councillors.

politics.q: Which city in Alsace is the official seat of the European Parliament?
politics.fact: Strasbourg is also home to the Council of Europe and the European Court of Human Rights.

politics.q: France was one of the six founding members of which organisation created by the 1957 Treaty of Rome?
politics.fact: The idea grew from French foreign minister Robert Schuman's declaration of 9 May 1950. The EU still marks 9 May as Europe Day.

politics.q: Who was President of France from 1974 to 1981?
politics.fact: In his first year in office, Giscard d'Estaing lowered the voting age in France from 21 to 18.

politics.q: Which French philosopher's "The Spirit of the Laws" (1748) argued for a separation of powers?
politics.fact: Montesquieu's ideas strongly influenced the framers of the United States Constitution.

politics.q: Which 1789 document begins "Men are born and remain free and equal in rights"?
choices: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
politics.fact: The Marquis de Lafayette drafted the Declaration with advice from Thomas Jefferson, then the American envoy in Paris.

politics.q: Which French President died in office in 1974?
politics.fact: The Centre Pompidou in Paris, the modern art centre with its pipes on the outside, is named after him. It opened in 1977.

politics.q: In which year did France pass its law separating the churches and the state?
politics.fact: The 1905 law is the cornerstone of "laïcité", the French principle that the state is neutral and does not recognise or fund any religion.

politics.q: Who became France's first female Prime Minister in 1991?
politics.fact: Cresson served for less than a year. More than 30 years later, Élisabeth Borne became the second woman to hold the post, in 2022.

politics.q: Which Auschwitz survivor became the first President of the directly elected European Parliament in 1979?
politics.fact: In 2018 Simone Veil was laid to rest in the Panthéon in Paris, only the fifth woman to be honoured there.

politics.q: Which Socialist served as Prime Minister under President Jacques Chirac from 1997 to 2002?
politics.fact: Jospin's government introduced the 35-hour working week in France.

politics.q: What is the French term for when the President and the Prime Minister come from opposing political camps?
politics.fact: The first cohabitation began in 1986, when Socialist President François Mitterrand appointed the Gaullist Jacques Chirac as Prime Minister.

current-affairs.q: Which city hosted the 2024 Summer Olympic Games?
current-affairs.fact: Paris also hosted the Games in 1900 and 1924, and became only the second city, after London, to host them three times.

current-affairs.q: Who won the French presidential election in 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Macron beat Marine Le Pen in the runoff and became the first French President to win re-election since Jacques Chirac in 2002.

current-affairs.q: In which year did Notre-Dame de Paris reopen after the 2019 fire?
current-affairs.fact: The April 2019 fire toppled the cathedral's 19th-century spire, designed by Viollet-le-Duc. The spire was rebuilt to the same design before the December 2024 reopening.

current-affairs.q: Which team beat France on penalties in the 2022 FIFA World Cup final?
current-affairs.fact: Kylian Mbappé scored a hat-trick in the final, the first in a men's World Cup final since England's Geoff Hurst in 1966.

current-affairs.q: Which French swimmer won four individual gold medals at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: On one evening Marchand won the 200m butterfly and the 200m breaststroke, about two hours apart, and the home crowd went wild.

current-affairs.q: Who became French Prime Minister in January 2024, the youngest in the history of the Fifth Republic?
current-affairs.fact: Attal was 34 when he was appointed. He had previously been Minister of Education.

current-affairs.q: France's 2023 pension reform raised the minimum retirement age from 62 to what?
current-affairs.fact: The government passed the reform using Article 49.3 of the constitution, which allows a bill through without a vote in the National Assembly. Mass protests followed.

current-affairs.q: Which country won the 2023 Rugby World Cup, held in France?
current-affairs.fact: South Africa beat New Zealand 12-11 in the final at the Stade de France, winning a record fourth Rugby World Cup.

current-affairs.q: In March 2024, France became the first country to explicitly guarantee which right in its constitution?
choices: The freedom to have an abortion
current-affairs.fact: Both houses of Parliament met together at the Palace of Versailles and approved the amendment by 780 votes to 72.

current-affairs.q: Which former EU chief Brexit negotiator was appointed French Prime Minister in September 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Barnier's government fell to a no-confidence vote in December 2024, after about three months. It was the first successful no-confidence vote since 1962.

current-affairs.q: Which French footballer won the 2022 Ballon d'Or?
current-affairs.fact: Benzema was the first Frenchman to win the Ballon d'Or since Zinedine Zidane in 1998.

current-affairs.q: Which club did Kylian Mbappé join in 2024 after leaving Paris Saint-Germain?
current-affairs.fact: Mbappé joined Real Madrid as a free agent when his PSG contract ended, and was welcomed by a packed crowd at the Bernabéu.

current-affairs.q: Along which river was the opening ceremony of the Paris 2024 Olympics held?
current-affairs.fact: It was the first opening ceremony of a Summer Games held outside a stadium. Athletes sailed about 6 km along the river on boats.

current-affairs.q: Which Canadian singer performed Édith Piaf's "Hymne à l'amour" from the Eiffel Tower at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony?
current-affairs.fact: It was Dion's first live performance since she revealed in 2022 that she has stiff-person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder.

current-affairs.q: In 2023 Forbes ranked Bernard Arnault as the world's richest person. Which luxury group does he head?
current-affairs.fact: LVMH owns brands such as Louis Vuitton, Dior and Moët & Chandon, and in 2021 it bought the jeweller Tiffany & Co.

current-affairs.q: Which striker overtook Thierry Henry in December 2022 to become France's all-time top goalscorer?
current-affairs.fact: Giroud retired from international football after Euro 2024 with 57 goals for France.

current-affairs.q: In June 2024, President Macron dissolved the National Assembly after his camp's heavy defeat in which vote?
current-affairs.fact: It was the first dissolution of the National Assembly since Jacques Chirac dissolved it in 1997.

current-affairs.q: Which French film won the Palme d'Or at the 2023 Cannes Film Festival?
choices: Portrait of a Lady on Fire
current-affairs.fact: Director Justine Triet became the third woman to win the Palme d'Or. The film later won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay.

current-affairs.q: Which two French sporting legends lit the Olympic cauldron at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony?
choices: Thierry Henry and Marie-Amélie Le Fur
current-affairs.fact: The cauldron was a ring lifted into the sky by a balloon in the Tuileries Garden. It used light and water mist instead of a real flame.

current-affairs.q: Which left-wing alliance won the most seats in France's snap legislative elections of July 2024?
current-affairs.fact: No group came close to a majority of the 577 seats, leaving France with a deeply divided National Assembly.

current-affairs.q: Who was appointed French Prime Minister in December 2024, after the fall of Michel Barnier's government?
current-affairs.fact: Bayrou, the founder of the centrist MoDem party, had run for President three times: in 2002, 2007 and 2012.

current-affairs.q: Which French writer won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Literature?
current-affairs.fact: Ernaux became the first French woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Her books draw closely on her own life and memories.

current-affairs.q: Which French scientist shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing CRISPR gene editing?
current-affairs.fact: Charpentier shared the prize with American Jennifer Doudna, the first time a science Nobel was shared by two women alone.

current-affairs.q: Who was appointed French Prime Minister in July 2020, succeeding Édouard Philippe?
current-affairs.fact: Castex had coordinated France's plan for lifting the first COVID-19 lockdown, earning him the nickname "Monsieur Déconfinement".

current-affairs.q: Which French physicist shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics for experiments on quantum entanglement?
current-affairs.fact: Aspect shared the prize with John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger. Their experiments confirmed that entangled particles behave as quantum theory predicts.

general.q: Which mountain on the France-Italy border is the highest in the Alps?
general.fact: Mont Blanc stands about 4,800 metres high, and its exact height changes slightly from year to year as its ice cap shifts.

general.q: Which famous three-week cycling race takes place in France every July?
general.fact: The Tour de France was first held in 1903. Since 1919, the overall race leader has worn the famous yellow jersey, the maillot jaune.

general.q: The Eiffel Tower was built as the entrance arch for which 1889 event?
choices: The end of the Franco-Prussian War
general.fact: The tower was only supposed to stand for 20 years. It was saved partly because it was useful as a giant radio antenna.

general.q: Which Mediterranean island is part of France?
general.fact: Corsica is nicknamed the "Île de Beauté" (Isle of Beauty). Many people there speak Corsican, a language closely related to Italian.

general.q: What is the longest river that flows entirely within France?
general.fact: The Loire flows for about 1,000 km. Part of its valley, famous for its Renaissance châteaux, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

general.q: What do the French call the English Channel?
general.fact: "La Manche" means "the sleeve", after the Channel's shape. The Channel Tunnel under it, about 50 km long, opened in 1994.

general.q: Because of its shape, what nickname do the French give to mainland France?
general.fact: "L'Hexagone" is so widely used that it often means mainland France as opposed to its overseas territories.

general.q: In which cathedral city were most French kings traditionally crowned?
general.fact: Reims is also at the heart of Champagne country. Many of the great Champagne houses age their wine in chalk cellars beneath the city.

general.q: Roquefort, one of France's most famous blue cheeses, is made from which animal's milk?
general.fact: To be called Roquefort, the cheese must be aged in the natural Combalou caves at Roquefort-sur-Soulzon. In 1925 it became the first French cheese with an AOC.

general.q: Which country shares France's longest land border?
general.fact: France's longest border, about 730 km, runs between its overseas region of French Guiana and Brazil in South America.

general.q: Which famous Paris avenue runs from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe?
general.fact: Every 14 July, France's national day, a grand military parade marches down the Champs-Élysées.

general.q: Which mountain range forms most of the border between France and Spain?
general.fact: The tiny country of Andorra sits in the Pyrenees. The French President is one of its two co-princes.

general.q: Which white-domed basilica stands on top of the hill of Montmartre in Paris?
general.fact: Montmartre is the highest natural point in Paris, about 130 metres above sea level, so the basilica can be seen from all over the city.

general.q: What is the French name for a long, thin loaf of bread with a crisp crust?
general.fact: In 2022 UNESCO added the craft and culture of the French baguette to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

general.q: Which rocky island off the coast of Normandy is crowned by a medieval abbey?
general.fact: The bay around Mont-Saint-Michel has some of the biggest tides in Europe, and the sea can sweep in across the sands very quickly.

general.q: Which city on the Mediterranean is France's largest seaport?
general.fact: Marseille was founded around 600 BC by Greek sailors from Phocaea, who called it Massalia. It is often called France's oldest city.

general.q: Which city, where the Rhône and Saône rivers meet, is often called the capital of French gastronomy?
general.fact: Lyon's old town is threaded with "traboules", hidden passageways through buildings once used by silk workers to carry their cloth.

general.q: What is the name of the strong, cold wind that blows down the Rhône valley to the Mediterranean?
general.fact: The Mistral often clears the sky of clouds, and painters have long praised the bright light it leaves behind in Provence.

general.q: Which Grand Slam tennis tournament is played on red clay in Paris each year?
general.fact: Its stadium, Roland-Garros, is named after the aviator Roland Garros, the first person to fly across the Mediterranean, in 1913.

general.q: Which wine-growing city on the Garonne gives its name to wines from the Médoc and Saint-Émilion?
general.fact: Bordeaux's elegant riverside, curved like a crescent, earned it the name "Port of the Moon". Much of the city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

general.q: Which landmark near Arcachon is the tallest sand dune in Europe?
general.fact: The Dune du Pilat rises more than 100 metres above the Atlantic, and the wind pushes it slowly inland every year.

general.q: What is the number of the Paris département, still used at the start of Paris postcodes?
general.fact: France's original départements were numbered roughly in alphabetical order, which is why Ain, in eastern France, is number 01.

general.q: Which Gothic cathedral south-west of Paris is famous for the deep "blue" of its medieval stained glass?
general.fact: Chartres still has most of its original 12th- and 13th-century stained glass, one of the largest such collections in the world.

general.q: Which 17th-century canal links Toulouse to the Mediterranean, forming part of a waterway between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean?
choices: The Canal du Rhône au Rhin
general.fact: Built between 1666 and 1681 by Pierre-Paul Riquet, the Canal du Midi became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.

general.q: What is the name of the Celtic language traditionally spoken in Brittany?
general.fact: Breton is closely related to Cornish and Welsh. It was brought to Brittany by Celtic settlers from Britain in the early Middle Ages.
